claim: UNC-3/Ebf is the terminal selector of C. elegans cholinergic motor neurons (MNs).
source: We previously showed that UNC-3/Ebf, the terminal selector of C. elegans cholinergic motor neurons (MNs), acts indirectly to prevent alternative neuronal identities (Feng et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript directly states this in the abstract with a citation to previous work.

claim: UNC-3 acts indirectly to prevent alternative neuronal identities.
source: We previously showed that UNC-3/Ebf, the terminal selector of C. elegans cholinergic motor neurons (MNs), acts indirectly to prevent alternative neuronal identities (Feng et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract with a citation to Feng et al., 2020.

claim: UNC-3 ChIP-Seq identified approximately 3500 protein-coding genes as putative direct targets.
source: Here, we employ chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by DNA sequencing (ChIP-Seq) and report the identification of ~3500 protein-coding genes as putative direct targets of UNC-3.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the number of targets identified through ChIP-Seq experiments.

claim: UNC-3 controls neuronal metabolism and downstream gene regulatory networks comprised of numerous TFs and nucleic acid-binding proteins.
source: Protein class ontology analysis suggests that UNC-3, besides terminal identity genes, also controls additional biological processes, such as neuronal metabolism and downstream gene regulatory networks comprised of numerous TFs and nucleic acid-binding proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract based on protein class ontology analysis of ChIP-Seq data.

claim: In all larval and adult stages examined, UNC-3 is required for continuous expression of various protein classes (e.g. receptors, transporters) critical for MN function.
source: In all larval and adult stages examined, UNC-3 is required for continuous expression of various protein classes (e.g. receptors, transporters) critical for MN function.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding from longitudinal analysis.

claim: Only in late larvae and adults, UNC-3 is required to maintain expression of MN-specific TFs.
source: However, only in late larvae and adults, UNC-3 is required to maintain expression of MN-specific TFs.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this temporal requirement for TF maintenance.

claim: The suite of UNC-3 targets in MNs is modified across different life stages, revealing 'temporal modularity' in terminal selector function.
source: Unexpectedly, we find that the suite of UNC-3 targets in MNs is modified across different life stages, revealing 'temporal modularity' in terminal selector function.
evidence: The abstract explicitly introduces the concept of temporal modularity based on the findings.

claim: Minimal disruption of UNC-3's temporal modularity via genome engineering affects locomotion.
source: Minimal disruption of UNC-3's temporal modularity via genome engineering affects locomotion.
evidence: The abstract states this finding from genome engineering experiments.

claim: UNC-30/Pitx, the terminal selector of GABAergic MN identity in C. elegans, also exhibits temporal modularity.
source: Another C. elegans terminal selector (UNC-30/Pitx) also exhibits temporal modularity, supporting the potential generality of this mechanism for the control of neuronal identity.
evidence: The abstract states this finding about UNC-30/Pitx.

claim: Terminal selectors are transcription factors (TFs) that establish during development and maintain throughout life post-mitotic neuronal identity.
source: Terminal selectors are transcription factors (TFs) that establish during development and maintain throughout life post-mitotic neuronal identity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a definition of terminal selectors.

claim: Terminal selectors activate the expression of effector genes whose protein products determine the terminally differentiated state and function of a given neuron type.
source: A defining feature of terminal selectors is the ability to activate the expression of effector genes, whose protein products determine the terminally differentiated state, and thereby function, of a given neuron type.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as a defining feature of terminal selectors.

claim: Terminal identity genes include neurotransmitter (NT) biosynthesis components, NT receptors, ion channels, neuropeptides, and adhesion molecules.
source: Examples include neurotransmitter (NT) biosynthesis components, NT receptors, ion channels, neuropeptides, and adhesion molecules (Hobert, 2008; Hobert, 2011; Hobert, 2016b).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations to support the examples.

claim: Multiple cases of terminal selectors have been described in worms, flies, chordates and mice.
source: Multiple cases of terminal selectors have been described thus far in worms, flies, chordates and mice (Deneris and Hobert, 2014; Hobert and Kratsios, 2019; Konstantinides et al., 2018), suggesting high conservation of this type of regulators.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations.

claim: Human mutations in terminal selectors and their effector target genes have been linked to either developmental or degenerative conditions of the nervous system.
source: Importantly, human mutations in terminal selectors and their effector target genes have been linked to either developmental or degenerative conditions of the nervous system (Deneris and Hobert, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with a citation.

claim: UNC-3 is the sole C. elegans ortholog of the Collier/Olf/Ebf (COE) family of TFs.
source: This study focuses on UNC-3, the sole C. elegans ortholog of the Collier/Olf/Ebf (COE) family of TFs (Dubois and Vincent, 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with a citation.

claim: Mutations in EBF3, a human ortholog of UNC-3, cause a neurodevelopmental syndrome characterized by motor developmental delay.
source: Importantly, mutations in EBF3, a human ortholog of UNC-3, cause a neurodevelopmental syndrome characterized by motor developmental delay (Blackburn et al., 2017; Chao et al., 2017; Harms et al., 2017; Sleven et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with multiple citations.

claim: UNC-3 controls cholinergic MN identity in C. elegans by activating directly the expression of various terminal identity genes.
source: A previous study proposed that UNC-3 controls cholinergic MN identity in C. elegans by activating directly the expression of various terminal identity genes (e.g., acetylcholine biosynthesis components, ion channels, NT receptors, neuropeptides), which were identified via a candidate approach (Kratsios et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with a citation to previous work.

claim: Animals lacking unc-3 gene activity display severe locomotion defects.
source: Lastly, animals lacking unc-3 gene activity display severe locomotion defects (Brenner, 1974; Feng et al., 2020), suggesting UNC-3 may broadly control gene expression in cholinergic MNs.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction with citations.

claim: The unc-3::gfp reporter strain faithfully recapitulates the endogenous unc-3 expression pattern.
source: Expression of UNC-3::GFP fusion protein was observed in the nucleus of 53 cholinergic MNs (SAB subtype = 3 neurons, DA = 9, DB = 7, VA = 12, VB = 11, AS = 11) and 19 other neurons known to express unc-3 (Figure 1A), indicating that this reporter faithfully recapitulates the endogenous unc-3 expression pattern (Pereira et al., 2015; Prasad et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 1A showing expression pattern.

claim: Insertion of GFP does not detectably alter the function of UNC-3.
source: Insertion of GFP does not detectably alter the function of UNC-3 since expression of known UNC-3 targets (cho-1/ChT, unc-17/VAChT, ace-2/AChE) is unaffected in unc-3::gfp animals (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantification in Figure 1B.

claim: unc-3::gfp animals do not display locomotion defects.
source: Unlike unc-3 null mutants, unc-3::gfp animals do not display locomotion defects.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation.

claim: ChIP-Seq for UNC-3 identified a total of 6892 unique binding peaks.
source: Our ChIP-Seq dataset revealed strong enrichment of UNC-3 binding in the genome by identifying a total of 6892 unique binding peaks (q-value cutoff: 0.05) (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 1C.

claim: The majority of UNC-3 binding peaks (91.95%) are predominantly located between 0 and 3 kb upstream of a transcription start site.
source: The majority of UNC-3 binding peaks (91.95%) are predominantly located between 0 and 3 kb upstream of a transcription start site, whereas only a small fraction is found in introns (2.05%) or downstream of a gene (0.99%), suggesting UNC-3 chiefly acts at promoters and enhancers to regulate gene expression (Figure 1D and F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with specific percentages and supported by Figure 1D and F.

claim: UNC-3 chiefly acts at promoters and enhancers to regulate gene expression.
source: The majority of UNC-3 binding peaks (91.95%) are predominantly located between 0 and 3 kb upstream of a transcription start site, whereas only a small fraction is found in introns (2.05%) or downstream of a gene (0.99%), suggesting UNC-3 chiefly acts at promoters and enhancers to regulate gene expression (Figure 1D and F).
evidence: This is inferred from the genomic distribution of binding peaks.

claim: A 12 bp pseudo-palindromic sequence was identified as the UNC-3 binding motif through de novo motif discovery analysis.
source: Through de novo motif discovery analysis (see Materials and methods), we identified a 12 bp pseudo-palindromic sequence overrepresented in the UNC-3 binding peaks (Figure 1E), which highly resembles the binding site of UNC-3 vertebrate orthologs (Treiber et al., 2010a; Treiber et al., 2010b; Wang and Reed, 1993; Wang et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1E with citations to support similarity to vertebrate orthologs.

claim: UNC-3 binding peaks are present in 9 out of 10 (90%) direct UNC-3 targets previously identified.
source: In the current study, we found UNC-3 binding peaks in 9 out of 10 (90%) direct UNC-3 targets and 38 of the 43 (88.37%) downstream targets of UNC-3, indicating high quality in the ChIP-Seq results (Figure 2A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with specific percentages and supported by Figure 2A.

claim: UNC-3 binding peaks are present in 38 of the 43 (88.37%) downstream targets of UNC-3 previously identified.
source: In the current study, we found UNC-3 binding peaks in 9 out of 10 (90%) direct UNC-3 targets and 38 of the 43 (88.37%) downstream targets of UNC-3, indicating high quality in the ChIP-Seq results (Figure 2A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with specific percentages.

claim: ChIP-Seq for UNC-3 appears highly sensitive, as it identified peaks in unc-3-dependent genes expressed in a limited number of neurons.
source: Moreover, ChIP-Seq for UNC-3 appears highly sensitive, as it identified peaks in unc-3-dependent genes expressed in a limited number of neurons (e.g., glr-4/GluR is expressed in 4 out of 72 unc-3+ neurons) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with an example and supported by Figure 2A.

claim: Bioinformatic analysis of the UNC-3 binding peaks revealed 3502 protein-coding genes as putative UNC-3 targets.
source: Our bioinformatic analysis of the UNC-3 binding peaks revealed 3502 protein-coding genes as putative UNC-3 targets (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Protein class ontology analysis revealed three broad categories of UNC-3 targets: terminal identity genes, gene expression regulators, and enzymes.
source: This analysis classifies UNC-3 targets into three broad categories: terminal identity genes, gene expression regulators, and enzymes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 42.18% of the total number of UNC-3 targets classified by PANTHER are terminal identity genes.
source: First, there is a preponderance (42.18% of the total number of UNC-3 targets classified by PANTHER) of terminal identity genes (e.g., 114 transporter proteins, 111 receptors and trans-membrane proteins, 37 signaling molecules, 11 cell adhesion molecules), suggesting that UNC-3 broadly affects multiple features of neuronal terminal identity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with specific percentages and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 24.07% of UNC-3 targets are proteins involved in the control of gene expression.
source: The second overrepresented category (24.07% of UNC-3 targets) contains a large number of proteins involved in the control of gene expression, such as 239 nucleic acid-binding proteins (16.77%) and 104 TFs (7.3%), highlighting the possibility of an extensive network of gene regulatory factors downstream of UNC-3.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with specific percentages and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 24.14% of UNC-3 targets are genes coding for various types of enzymes.
source: The third category (24.14%) consists of genes coding for various types of enzymes (e.g., hydrolases, ligases, oxidoreductases), suggesting a new role for UNC-3 in neuronal metabolic pathways.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with specific percentages and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 52.95% of MN-expressed genes identified by single-cell RNA-Seq are bound by UNC-3.
source: We found that 52.95% of these MN-expressed genes are bound by UNC-3 and fall in the aforementioned gene categories (Supplementary file 3), thereby constituting putative UNC-3 targets in cholinergic MNs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on comparison with CeNGEN single-cell RNA-Seq data.

claim: 10 of 16 randomly selected TF reporters were sufficient to drive RFP expression in ventral cord MNs.
source: We generated transgenic reporter animals and found that 10 of these TF reporters were sufficient to drive RFP expression in ventral cord MNs (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and summarized in Table 1.

claim: 9 TFs (nhr-1, nhr-40, mab-9, ztf-26, ceh-44, zfh-2, cfi-1, bnc-1, nhr-19) have expression in cholinergic MNs.
source: Next, we identified 9 TFs (nhr-1, nhr-40, mab-9, ztf-26, ceh-44, zfh-2, cfi-1, bnc-1, nhr-19) with expression in cholinergic MNs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on reporter analysis.

claim: 8 of the 9 TF reporters with expression in cholinergic MNs are positively regulated by unc-3.
source: Next, we tested for unc-3 dependency at the L4 stage, and found that 8 of the 9 TF reporters (nhr-1, nhr-40, zfh-2, ztf-26, ceh-44, cfi-1, bnc-1, mab-9) with expression in cholinergic MNs are positively regulated by unc-3; their expression significantly decreased in unc-3 mutants (Table 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: nhr-49 is negatively regulated by unc-3; ectopic expression was observed in cholinergic MNs of unc-3 mutants.
source: On the other hand, nhr-49, which is normally expressed in GABAergic MNs, is negatively regulated by unc-3; ectopic expression was observed in cholinergic MNs of unc-3 mutants (Table 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Table 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Four terminal identity genes (acr-2/AChR, unc-129/TGFbeta, glr-4/GluR, unc-17/VAChT) critically depend on UNC-3 at every stage (L2, L4, day 1 adult).
source: First, we tested four terminal identity genes (acr-2/AChR, unc-129/TGFbeta, glr-4/GluR, unc-17/VAChT) at larval (L2, L4) and adult (day 1) stages and found that their MN expression, at every stage, critically depends on UNC-3 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: UNC-3 is continuously required to maintain expression of terminal identity genes acr-2/AChR, glr-4/GluR, and unc-17/VAChT.
source: Compared to controls, we found a significant decrease in the number of adult MNs expressing acr-2/AChR, glr-4/GluR, and unc-17/VAChT in animals treated with auxin (Figure 3—figure supplement 2). These findings indicate UNC-3 is required to initiate and maintain the expression of terminal identity genes, consolidating its role as a terminal selector of cholinergic MN fate.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on auxin-inducible degradation experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Three TFs (zfh-2/Zfhx3, ztf-26, nhr-1) critically depend on UNC-3 at every stage (L2, L4, adult).
source: Similar to terminal identity genes, the expression of 3 TFs (zfh-2/Zfhx3, ztf-26, nhr-1) critically depends on UNC-3 at every stage (L2, L4, adult) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting UNC-3 controls initiation and maintenance of their expression.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The early expression (L2 stage) of five TFs (cfi-1, bnc-1, mab-9, nhr-40, ceh-44) does not require UNC-3.
source: In striking contrast, the early expression (L2 stage) of five TFs (cfi-1, bnc-1, mab-9, nhr-40, ceh-44) does not require UNC-3 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Maintenance of expression of five TFs (cfi-1, bnc-1, mab-9, nhr-40, ceh-44) during late larval and/or adult stages depends on UNC-3.
source: However, maintenance of their expression during late larval and/or adult stages does depend on UNC-3 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A 2.5 kb distal element (reporter #7) is sufficient for embryonic (3-fold stage) MN expression of cfi-1.
source: Surprisingly, this analysis did not reveal a separate initiation element. Instead, it showed that the same 2.5 kb distal element (reporter #7) that drives RFP expression in subsets of unc-3-expressing cholinergic MNs (DA, DB, VA, VB subtypes) at larval and adult stages (Figure 3B), is also sufficient for embryonic (3-fold stage) MN expression (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: A 769 bp sequence within the 2.5 kb enhancer is required for both initiation and maintenance of cfi-1 in nerve cord MNs.
source: Genome editing suggests that a 769 bp sequence within this 2.5 kb enhancer is required for both initiation and maintenance of cfi-1 in nerve cord MNs (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on CRISPR deletion experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Eight putative UNC-3 binding sites (COE motifs) were identified within the 769 bp distal enhancer of cfi-1.
source: Through bioinformatic analysis (see Materials and methods), we identified eight putative UNC-3 binding sites (COE motifs) within the 769 bp distal enhancer (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Mutation of all eight COE motifs in the cfi-1 enhancer does not affect early cfi-1 expression (L2 stage) but significantly down-regulates expression at later larval (L4) and adult (day 1) stages.
source: During the L2 stage, expression of mNG in MNs is not affected in mNG::AID::cfi-1 8 COE motifs mut animals, indicating early cfi-1 expression occurs normally (Figure 4F). Intriguingly, mNG expression is significantly down-regulated in cholinergic MNs at later larval (L4) and adult (day 1) stages, resembling the phenotype of unc-3 null mutants (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4F.

claim: UNC-3 binds to the distal enhancer and directly acts through one or more of the 8 COE motifs to maintain cfi-1 expression in cholinergic MNs.
source: We conclude that UNC-3 binds to the distal enhancer and directly acts through one or more of these 8 COE motifs to maintain cfi-1 expression in cholinergic MNs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the COE motif mutation experiments.

claim: cfi-1 does not auto-regulate.
source: We found though that cfi-1 does not auto-regulate and UNC-3 binding at the distal enhancer occurs normally in cfi-1 null mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), excluding a potential involvement of CFI-1 in its own maintenance.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: LIN-39 (Scr/Dfd/HOX4-5) and MAB-5 (Antp/HOX6-8) control cfi-1 expression in MNs.
source: Previous work showed that two Hox proteins, LIN-39 (Scr/Dfd/HOX4-5) and MAB-5 (Antp/HOX6-8), control cfi-1 expression in MNs (Kratsios et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to previous work.

claim: Expression of the endogenous mNG::AID::cfi-1 reporter in cholinergic MNs is severely affected at embryonic (3-fold), larval (L2, L4) and adult (D1) stages in lin-39; mab-5 double null mutants.
source: Because lin-39; mab-5 double null mutants are viable (Liu and Fire, 2000), we performed a longitudinal analysis and found that expression of the endogenous mNG::AID::cfi-1 reporter in cholinergic MNs is severely affected at embryonic (3-fold), larval (L2, L4) and adult (D1) stages (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: LIN-39 and MAB-5 are required for cfi-1 initiation.
source: Since onset of cfi-1 expression occurs at the 3-fold embryonic stage (Figure 4B), these results suggest LIN-39 and MAB-5 are required for cfi-1 initiation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the longitudinal analysis.

claim: LIN-39 and MAB-5 bind to the cfi-1 distal enhancer.
source: Moreover, available ChIP-Seq data from modENCODE (Boyle et al., 2014) indicate that LIN-39 and MAB-5 bind to the cfi-1 distal enhancer (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Expression of a 2.5 kb transgenic cfi-1 reporter (reporter #7) is significantly affected in lin-39; mab-5 double mutants at early larval (L2) stages.
source: Expression of a 2.5 kb transgenic cfi-1 reporter (reporter #7) that carries the distal enhancer is significantly affected in lin-39; mab-5 double mutants at early larval (L2) stages (Figure 5A,D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A and D.

claim: Mutation of a single LIN-39 binding site within the cfi-1 enhancer led to a decrease in reporter gene expression at L2.
source: Although the DNA sequence of the MAB-5 binding site is not known, mutation of a single, bioinformatically predicted LIN-39 binding site (wild-type: aaTTGAtg >mutated: aaGGGGtg) within the enhancer led to a decrease in reporter gene expression at L2 (Figure 5A,E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A and E.

claim: LIN-39 and MAB-5 act synergistically because endogenous cfi-1 expression is mildly affected in lin-39 single mutants, but severely affected in lin-39; mab-5 double mutants.
source: Indeed, LIN-39 and MAB-5 appear to act synergistically because endogenous cfi-1 expression (mNG::AID::cfi-1) is mildly affected in lin-39 single mutants, but severely affected in lin-39; mab-5 double mutants (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The Hox proteins LIN-39 and MAB-5 are necessary for cfi-1 initiation in cholinergic MNs.
source: We conclude that the Hox proteins LIN-39 and MAB-5 are necessary for cfi-1 initiation in cholinergic MNs (left panel, Figure 5G), and act through the same distal enhancer utilized by UNC-3 to maintain cfi-1 (right panel, Figure 5G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion and shown in Figure 5G.

claim: LIN-39 and MAB-5 act through the same distal enhancer utilized by UNC-3 to maintain cfi-1.
source: We conclude that the Hox proteins LIN-39 and MAB-5 are necessary for cfi-1 initiation in cholinergic MNs (left panel, Figure 5G), and act through the same distal enhancer utilized by UNC-3 to maintain cfi-1 (right panel, Figure 5G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion and shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Mutation of the LIN-39 binding site within the cfi-1 enhancer led to a sustained decrease in reporter gene expression from L2 to adult stages.
source: Supporting a maintenance role for Hox, mutation of the LIN-39 binding site within the cfi-1 enhancer (reporter #8) led to a sustained decrease in reporter gene expression from L2 to adult stages (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5E.

claim: CFI-1 is required during early development to establish the identity of DA and DB subtypes by acting as a transcriptional repressor.
source: Although its function in VA and VB remains unknown, CFI-1 is required during early development to establish the identity of DA and DB subtypes by acting as a transcriptional repressor (Kerk et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation.

claim: In cfi-1 null animals, glutamate receptor subunit 4 (glr-4/GluR) becomes ectopically expressed in DA and DB neurons.
source: In cfi-1 null animals, glutamate receptor subunit 4 (glr-4/GluR), a terminal identity gene normally activated by UNC-3 in another MN subtype (SAB), becomes ectopically expressed in DA and DB neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: CFI-1 is required post-embryonically to continuously prevent DA and DB from obtaining a mixed identity.
source: At the L3 stage (2 days upon continuous auxin treatment), we observed ectopic expression of glr-4 in DA and DB neurons. These results suggest that CFI-1 is required post-embryonically to prevent DA and DB neurons from adopting mixed identity, underscoring the critical role of UNC-3 and Hox in maintaining cfi-1 expression (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on auxin-inducible degradation experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Animals carrying the mNG::AID::cfi-1 8 COE motifs mut allele display locomotion defects.
source: Compared to cfi-1 null mutants, animals carrying the mNG::AID::cfi-1 8 COE motifs mut allele (selective disruption of cfi-1 maintenance) display milder, but statistically significant locomotion defects in the adult (Figure 6B–G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6B-G.

claim: Minimal disruption of temporal modularity in UNC-3 function can affect animal behavior.
source: This analysis suggests that minimal disruption of temporal modularity in UNC-3 function can affect animal behavior.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the locomotion analysis.

claim: LIN-39 and MAB-5 are required for bnc-1 expression at all stages examined (L2, L4, day 1 adult).
source: Using an endogenous reporter allele (bnc-1::mNG::AID), we found that LIN-39 and MAB-5 are required for bnc-1 expression at all stages examined (L2, L4, day 1 adult; Figure 5—figure supplement 3), suggesting a role for Hox in bnc-1 initiation and maintenance.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: UNC-3 is absolutely required for bnc-1 maintenance in the adult (day 1).
source: Next, we found that UNC-3 is absolutely required for bnc-1 maintenance in the adult (day 1), albeit weaker effects were also observed at L2 and L4 (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: UNC-30/PITX is the terminal selector of GABAergic MN (DD, VD) identity in the C. elegans nerve cord.
source: To address this, we focused on UNC-30/PITX, the terminal selector of GABAergic MN (DD, VD) identity in the C. elegans nerve cord (Figure 7A; Jin et al., 1994).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Terminal identity gene (unc-25/GAD, unc-47/VGAT) expression is affected in GABAergic MNs of unc-30 mutants at all stages examined (3-fold embryo, L2, L4, adult [day 1]).
source: Using reporter strains and methodologies similar to those used for UNC-3, we found that terminal identity gene (unc-25/GAD, unc-47/VGAT) expression is affected in GABAergic MNs of unc-30 mutants at all stages examined (3-fold embryo, L2, L4, adult [day 1]) (Figure 7B,D), suggesting a requirement for initiation and maintenance.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7B and D.

claim: In GABAergic MNs, UNC-30/PITX is selectively required for the maintenance, but not initiation of cfi-1 expression.
source: We found no effect at the embryonic stage (3-fold), but progressively stronger effects at larval (L2, L4) and adult (day 1) stages (Figure 7C), indicating that, in GABAergic MNs, UNC-30/PITX is selectively required for the maintenance, but not initiation of cfi-1 expression.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The function of UNC-30 in GABAergic MNs is organized into two modules (module #1: initiation and maintenance; module #2: maintenance-only).
source: Taken together, our findings indicate that, like UNC-3 in cholinergic MNs (Figure 3C), the function of UNC-30 in GABAergic MNs is organized into two modules (module #1: initiation and maintenance; module #2: maintenance-only) (Figure 7D–E), suggesting temporal modularity may be a shared feature among terminal selector type-TFs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7D-E.

claim: UNC-30 binds to the same distal enhancer of cfi-1 in GABAergic MNs, as UNC-3 does in cholinergic MNs.
source: UNC-30 also binds to the same distal enhancer of cfi-1 in GABAergic MNs, as UNC-3 does in cholinergic MNs (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The UNC-30 binding sites are distinct from the UNC-3 sites in the cfi-1 enhancer.
source: However, the UNC-30 binding sites are distinct from the UNC-3 sites in this enhancer (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Maintenance of cfi-1 expression in two different neuron types relies on the same enhancer receiving UNC-30/PITX input in GABAergic MNs and UNC-3/EBF input in cholinergic MNs.
source: This finding suggests that maintenance of cfi-1 expression in two different neuron types relies on the same enhancer receiving UNC-30/PITX input in GABAergic MNs and UNC-3/EBF input in cholinergic MNs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the data.

claim: The cfi-1 enhancer provides an example of 'enhancer pleiotropy', in which the same cis-regulatory element is used to control gene expression in different neuron types.
source: Interestingly, these results provide an example of 'enhancer pleiotropy' (Sabarís et al., 2019), in which the same cis-regulatory element is used to control gene expression in different neuron types.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation.

claim: Temporal modularity in terminal selector function is necessary for generating and maintaining neuronal subtype diversity.
